articles.title: Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) Latest News - Vajiram & Ravi
articles.summary: Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) Latest News  Vajiram & Ravi
articles.full_text:
- The United States Trade Representative (USTR) has launched an investigation into the European Union’s expansion of its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) — a move that could escalate trade tensions between the two blocs.
- The USTR has invited public comments from American small businesses till November 9. Seeking public comments is typically the first step toward possible retaliation — signalling the US may push the EU to soften CBAM’s implementation.
- For India, this development carries an unusual silver lining: any US-driven softening of CBAM could automatically benefit Indian exporters too, thanks to a clause in the India-EU trade deal.
What Is CBAM, and Why Is the US Investigating It?
- CBAM is the EU’s carbon pricing mechanism. It requires EU importers of goods in six carbon-intensive sectors to declare the embedded emissions of imported products and pay a carbon price equivalent to what EU domestic producers already pay.
- Covered Sectors: Aluminium; Cement; Electricity; Fertiliser; Hydrogen; Iron and steel.
The US’s Specific Complaint
- The EU calculates default emission values using country- and sector-level production/energy data.
- However, the EU adds a punitive mark-up to these default values — a measure meant to push companies toward submitting verified company-level data instead.
- Any company-level data must be verified by an EU-accredited third-party verifier — adding cost and compliance burden, which the US says disproportionately hurts American small businesses.
How India Stands to Benefit
- India had tough negotiations with the EU over CBAM while finalising the India-EU trade deal, since the regulation is expected to hit a wide range of Indian metal exports.
- Crucially, however, Indian negotiators secured a ‘forward-Most Favoured Nation’ (MFN) CBAM clause.
- What this clause does – It ensures that any concession the EU grants to another trading partner (here, the US) under a separate agreement automatically extends to India too.
  - In the EU-US trade deal joint statement (August last year), the EU had already committed: “…the European Commission… commits to work to provide additional flexibilities in the CBAM implementation” for US businesses.
  - If the ongoing USTR probe results in further CBAM flexibilities for the US, India would also receive those same concessions — without needing to renegotiate separately.
The Stakes for Indian Industry
- According to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), CBAM could translate into a 20–35% tax on select Indian exports — particularly iron, steel, and aluminium — into the EU.
- This is effectively being called a steel bill for India.
- Added complication — Steel Scrap
  - The EU is the world’s largest producer of steel scrap, and its move to curb steel-scrap exports, combined with CBAM, acts as a non-tariff barrier against Indian industry.
  - Despite Indian objections, the EU kept CBAM outside the scope of the India-EU trade deal.
- Why Production Method Matters
  - Blast furnace–basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF) route: highest emissions.
  - Gas-based direct reduced iron (DRI): lower emissions.
  - Scrap-based electric arc furnace (EAF) route: lowest emissions.
- India’s Vulnerability: Indian manufacturers largely rely on the blast furnace route, making them currently underprepared for CBAM’s carbon-price burden.
India’s Response: The Green Steel Push
- The government plans to scale up scrap-based steel production via electric arc furnace technology, under its Green Steel Initiative.
- However, a May 2025 report by the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER) flagged a major constraint:
  - Scrap currently makes up only 20% of India’s steelmaking feedstock.
  - This is limited by domestic scrap availability of just ~25 Million Metric Tonnes (MMt) annually.
  - The report notes: hard-to-abate sectors like steel face unprecedented pressure to decarbonise amid tools like CBAM, with scrap steel central to this transition — yet India’s constrained scrap access remains a critical bottleneck.
Conclusion
- The US probe into CBAM is, at its core, a dispute over how the EU prices carbon at its borders — but it has inadvertently opened a door for India.
- Thanks to a carefully negotiated MFN clause, any flexibility the EU grants the US could flow to Indian exporters too, without further bargaining.
- Yet this remains a short-term cushion, not a solution: India’s long-term competitiveness in a carbon-taxed world will depend on how fast it can scale scrap-based, low-emission steel production — a transition still constrained by domestic scrap scarcity.

articles.title: Russia lost more than 50,000 troops in a month, Ukraine 10 times fewer — NATO - Українські Національні Новини (УНН)
articles.summary: Russia lost more than 50,000 troops in a month, Ukraine 10 times fewer — NATO  Українські Національні Новини (УНН)
articles.full_text:
Kyiv • UNN
According to NATO's assessment, Russia lost more than 50,000 troops in September, while Ukraine lost around 5,000. The figures have not been independently verified.
In September 2026, the Russian army suffered more than 50,000 military personnel killed and wounded in Ukraine. Of these, up to 28,000 were killed. Bloomberg reports this, citing a senior NATO military official, writes UNN.
Details
According to the Alliance official's estimates, Ukrainian forces lost around 5,000 military personnel over the same period. Thus, according to these estimates, the Russian army's total losses were approximately 10 times higher.
The publication's source explained that the Russian command continues to send its units on the offensive through so-called kill zones, where troops come under strikes from drones and artillery and encounter minefields.
The war is becoming increasingly costly for Russia
According to Bloomberg, Ukrainian forces have also intensified strikes on facilities deep inside Russia, including oil refineries and data centers. At the same time, during ground operations, the Defense Forces regained control of more than 125 square kilometers of territory.
Against the backdrop of significant losses, the Russian authorities continue to increase military spending. In 2026, Russia's defense budget is expected to reach 17 trillion rubles, or approximately $199 billion. This is 40% more than the initial plan presented at the end of 2025.
At the same time, the Kremlin is not publishing official data on the losses suffered by its army or the scale of recruitment of new military personnel. It is currently impossible to independently verify NATO's estimates.

articles.title: 'Up to our people' to pick leader, Zelenskyy responds to Trump's pledge for new elections in Ukraine - Euronews.com
articles.summary: 'Up to our people' to pick leader, Zelenskyy responds to Trump's pledge for new elections in Ukraine  Euronews.com'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal  BBCBritain stands behind Zelenskyy, says Streeting after Trump’s call for new leader in Ukraine  The GuardianZelensky repeats offer to hold elections if Russia agrees to ceasefire  The TimesGermany backs Ukraine's Zelenskiy after Trump's call for his remova...
articles.full_text:
Only Russia is responsible for the war in Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday in a TV interview, responding to criticism from US President Donald Trump, who blamed him for high diesel prices and said he should be replaced.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday his country could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire, pushing back against US counterpart Donald Trump's call for Ukraine to pick a new leader.
"First of all, with all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader", Zelenskyy told ABC News in a televised interview, a day after Trump said Ukraine needed a new president who would agree to end the war.
Zelenskyy said he told Trump's team that if they really wanted Ukraine to hold elections, "please tell Putin to give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections".
"We want peace, we are ready for a ceasefire, we are ready to begin with any kind of steps of de-escalation", Zelenskyy told ABC in a TV interview.
"And if the Russians want us not to attack their diesel, their refineries, etc., we are asking President Trump to give them a signal not to attack the energy infrastructure of Ukraine".
'Don't kill our children, we will stop attacking your diesel'
The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data centre run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than four and a half years after Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
"It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so", Zelenskyy said on X, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees.
"Don't attack us. Don't kill our children. We will stop attacking your diesel. And I think it's a fair deal", he added.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Trump's comments, writing on X late Saturday that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence. "He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well", Sybiha wrote.
Trump vows for 'new leader' in Ukraine
Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does", Trump said.
The US president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.

articles.title: Could student protests ignite a wider movement in France? - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Could student protests ignite a wider movement in France?  Euronews.comAngry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know why | Kitty Sayers  The GuardianFrance promises 3,000 extra teachers in first step to calm student protests  BBCArson at the school gate and tear gas on the streets  The EconomistFrench mayor caught in viral video clash says student protesters 'could be my children'  Reuters
articles.full_text:
French students' grievances include long school days, overcrowded classrooms, outdated facilities and teacher shortages. Their anger has resonated across Europe, with students in Belgium and Italy also staging protests.
Three weeks into France’s student protests, questions are mounting over whether the demonstrations will fizzle out or evolve into a broader social movement.
The protests and school blockades began in Paris’s suburbs in mid-September, before rapidly spreading nationwide. Dramatic images of students climbing the iconic column at Paris' Place de la Bastille on Thursday managed to capture audiences worldwide.
The scenes carried historical weight given that the square stands on the site of the former Bastille fortress and state prison, stormed by Parisians on 14 July 1789 in a defining moment of the French Revolution.
After its demolition, the Bastille became a lasting symbol of the triumph of regular citizens against political oppression. Taking to X on Thursday, hard-left France Unbowed leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon declared that the Bastille had been "retaken."
A range of student grievances lie at the heart of the movement, including long school days, overcrowded classrooms, run down schools and teacher absences. Their anger has resonated with young people across Europe, with students in Belgium and Italy also staging protests in recent days.
Could the student movement grow into something broader?
Another day of protests, backed by student and trade unions, is scheduled for Tuesday, 13 October. Meanwhile, a separate demonstration against the cost of living crisis and rising fuel prices — planned before the student movement erupted — is scheduled for 17 October.
There is speculation that the 17 October demonstration could mark the return of the yellow vest grassroots movement, which emerged in 2018 in reaction to a planned government fuel and diesel tax hike. For months, yellow vest protestors gathered every weekend to block roundabouts, motorways, and fuel depots across the country, with tense police clashes also occurring.
If student protests converge with wider social unrest, France could potentially face scenes reminiscent of May 1968. In recent weeks, many students have brandished banners referencing these historic demonstrations, which saw student protests escalate into a nationwide general strike.
At the time, several million workers joined the demonstrations, bringing the country to a standstill, but also sparking major wage negotiations. The movement also triggered a political crisis, prompting General de Gaulle, then France's president, to dissolve the National Assembly and call snap legislative elections in June 1968, in which his supporters secured a parliamentary majority.
Regardless, May 1968 left an indelible mark on France by dismantling rigid post-war social hierarchies. The demonstrations helped advance civil, student and labour rights, permanently embedding a tradition of mass protest into the nation's political identity.
France's tense political backdrop
At present, France's minority government is struggling to secure parliamentary support for its 2027 budget, as opposition parties resist proposed austerity measures. The country's public finances are squeezed, with the government projecting the public deficit to reach 5.4% of GDP for 2026, among the highest level in the eurozone.
The deepening cost-of-living crisis, driven largely by high fuel and energy prices, has intensified public frustration. The economic pressure on households has heightened social tensions across the country, less than six months away from the country's presidential elections — amid a highly fragmented political landscape.
According to a poll by public polling firm Ifop, carried out between 25 and 29 September, the far-right National Rally party's Marine Le Pen (35%) is currently leading for the first round, followed by Edouard Philippe (15%) and Jean-Luc Mélenchon (14%). Under these projections, the second round would see a Le Pen-Philippe face off. Other projections have predicted a Le Pen vs Mélenchon scenario for the second round.
A movement which shows no sign of abating
Despite Education Minister Édouard Geffray's announcement on Thursday that 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed nationwide to schools facing teacher shortages, public anger shows little sign of abating. Geffray said the measure would likely cost “tens of millions of euros” for 2026.
Unions have criticised the plan as a short-term fix, warning that available substitute teachers may not match schools' needs in terms of specialisms or location. In cases where no replacement is available, classes may still go uncovered, while substitute teachers may be assigned support duties until a matching vacancy arises.
“We need to look at the details, because we have to be careful with this figure that has been thrown around," Jean-Rémi Girard, a teacher and president of the national union of schools and higher education (SNALC) told Euronews.
From the onset, students have been supported by teaching unions, as Girard pointed to a system in "crisis."
"We are increasingly struggling to replace teacher absences, French classrooms are among the most crowded in Europe, classrooms aren't properly equipped during heat waves. These are things we already know."
"The starting point is that the school system is in crisis, and it has been for a long time."
Major trade union federations in France have also rallied alongside students. Following Thursday's protests, the CGT, one of the country's largest trade unions, highlighted a range of demonstrations, some of which were unrelated to the student movement, declaring: "The struggles are multiplying, and the balance of power is shifting!"
Parallels with past student protests in France
Paolo Stuppia, professor of sociology and politics at Sciences Po Paris, drew parallels between the current demonstrations and past social movements in France, citing a range of movements including May 1968.
"It’s not new for students from the suburbs to rally around demands that are specific to them, and then for those demands to be taken up by other secondary schools located closer to the city centre."
For Stuppia, the fact that students from private schools have also participated in blockades marks a new departure for student protest movements. Many observers were also surprised that students from the Université Paris-Panthéon-Assas, which is viewed as having a conservative student body, staged a blockade on Thursday.
Nevertheless, Stuppia warned that the movement's momentum could be impacted by upcoming school half-term holidays in France.
"When there’s a two-week school break, it becomes harder to get a movement going again afterwards, because everything has been on hold."
A movement which has expanded in response to police violence
While many demonstrations have been peaceful, others have been marred by sideline riots and clashes with law enforcement authorities. According to figures shared by France's Ministry of Justice on Friday, there have been 6,877 arrests since the beginning of the movement, with 86% involving minors.
The scale of arrests is striking compared with those made in the initial weeks of the yellow vest movement in 2018, which saw 4,596 people placed in police custody during its first month.
Rights groups have condemned police brutality following a wave of shocking injuries to students.
Outrage has grown over cases including a 15-year-old schoolboy who lost his left hand to a police stun grenade, a 16-year-old partially blinded by a rubber bullet, and a 14-year-old who suffered a shattered jaw and lost multiple teeth after being struck by a tear gas canister. The incidents are under internal investigation, with a total of 24 currently being conducted by the French police disciplinary body.
A United Nations spokesperson declared on Friday that the organisation was concerned about the situation in France, calling for demonstrations to remain peaceful and for the use of force to be proportionate.
Meanwhile, according to authorities, 761police officers and gendarmes have been injured since the beginning of the protests. Across the country, several schools have been damaged, burned or ransacked. In some cases, rioters have infiltrated the demonstrations.
For Stuppia, the level of police repression in recent weeks was "unprecedented" since May 1968 protests.
Meanwhile, Valérie Becquet, a sociologist at CY Cergy Paris University and co-author with Paolo Stuppia of "Geopolitics of Youth: Engagement and (e)Mobilisation", said police brutality has helped draw adults into the movement.
"Adults [trade unions and parents] have been marching alongside students, but have also intervened through contacting lawyers and magistrates, in response to violence and possible human rights violations."
However, she said that there was also a portion of the adult population which viewed the protests with "disdain" and "dismissed or discredited" them.
Increasingly politicised protests
In a TV address on Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu lamented the “violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalised, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults.”
He took aim at “political leaders who use this anger to conduct their electoral battles.” France goes to the polls for a presidential election in April. “We cannot play with the safety of France’s youth,” Lecornu said.

articles.title: The bond crisis is about to ripple out into the real economy - The Telegraph
articles.summary: The bond crisis is about to ripple out into the real economy  The TelegraphFrance’s dilemma: protesters demand spending as markets require fiscal restraint  The GuardianEurope’s Indebted Nations Are Starting to Blink at Market Wrath  Yahoo FinanceFrance’s Bond Turmoil Raises the Specter of Contagion in Europe  Bloomberg.comNobel winner Krugman says France may have become 'too big to save'  CNBC
articles.full_text:
Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, is frantically trying to cap rates. France may be about to trigger a fresh eurozone crisis. And here in Britain, John Healey, the new Chancellor, is facing what his predecessor would no doubt have described as a “black hole” in the public finances.
As bond yields – the cost of borrowing – rise relentlessly, so far all the attention has focused on the effect on hugely indebted governments. But the crisis is about to ripple out into the real economy – and, unfortunately, that will prove a lot more serious.
It has been hard to escape the rising cost of government debt right around the world. American 30-year Treasury yields hit 5.7pc this week, the highest level since 2002.
France’s 10-year yields are close to 5pc, the highest level since before the euro-zone crisis in 2010. Here in Britain, 30-year yields have punched through the 6pc barrier, the highest since 1998. You need a very long memory to remember when money last cost this much.
We are already starting to see the effect of that on government finances that were already strained to breaking point. Only this week, it was estimated that the rising cost of servicing Britain’s £3tn of debt meant that the Chancellor’s fiscal headroom had shrunk by £11bn, and that may force him into tax rises and spending cuts in the Budget later this month. Every other finance minister is facing the same difficult choices.
The trouble is, that is not the real problem. At the end of the day, a government can always raise taxes if it is forced to, and a central bank can print money if there are no other options.
It starts to get genuinely worrying when those soaring yields start to impact the rest of the economy. After all, government debt is the benchmark against which every other financial instrument is measured. When the cost goes up, so does everything else.
That will hurt in three main ways. To start with, mortgage rates are starting to rise. The average five-year fixed rate hit 6pc in Britain this week, and is still climbing.
We may be back at double-digit rates before too long. That is going to hit a housing market that is already starting to weaken, and which at the top end, in London and the South-East, is now in freefall. When house prices start to fall, as we know from bitter experience, some of the smaller mortgage lenders start to run into trouble, as well as the estate agents, builders, decorating shops and all the other businesses and trades that depend on a healthy property market.
We have no real idea what will happen to people who fixed their rates at 1pc when they have to refinance at 7pc or 8pc. But here is a guess. It is not going to be pretty.
Next, don’t count on the banks and pension funds coming through unscathed. Every kind of financial institution inevitably holds a lot of government debt. Indeed, many of them are required by their regulators to do so. As yields soar, there are bigger and bigger losses on their existing portfolio that will eventually have to be accounted for.
The banks will have to put aside more capital to meet any markdowns on their bond portfolio and that will mean they can lend less as well. When credit dries up, a recession is seldom far behind.
Finally, there will be a huge impact on corporate lending. Ironically, in over-indebted France, companies can now borrow at cheaper rates than an almost bankrupt state, and the same may soon be true in Britain as well. Even so, the cost of corporate debt will inevitably rise.
Just about every company has some form of borrowing, and they will very soon be paying a lot more to finance that. That means there will be less money left over for salaries, investment or dividends for their shareholders, especially as the Government will probably be raising their taxes again.
Even more seriously, the large number of private equity deals struck when money cost just 1pc will be in big trouble when they have to refinance at 6pc.
There are an estimated 13,000 businesses in Britain owned by private equity firms. Many of the biggest buyouts, such as Asda and Morrisons, were already in a dire state even when money was still cheap. A lot of the private equity deals are going to be in even more trouble once they have to refinance all that borrowing.
Of course, it will take time for all that to be felt. The majority of mortgages in the UK, along with corporate and private equity borrowing, are fixed. It will be a few months before all those rates start to go up. But just because something is delayed does not mean it is not going to happen.
In reality, we may soon face a steep downturn in the property market, a collapse in bank lending, and plenty of over-indebted companies running into trouble, with some even forced to close.
Worst of all, that will reduce tax revenues even further, forcing the Government to increase borrowing, which will push rates even higher. The economy will be trapped in a vicious cycle from which there will be no easy escape.
Lots of people will tell you that the cost of money is just getting back to its long-term levels. There is plenty of truth in that. By any historical standards, a 5pc or 6pc yield is nothing unusual.
The issue is that 15 years of ultra-cheap borrowing is going to be very painful to unwind. The bond crisis will start to hit the real economy in the next six months – and that will be very ugly.

articles.title: Negotiations between Ukraine, Europe, and the U.S. in Miami ended without a breakthrough — media reports - UA.NEWS
articles.summary: Negotiations between Ukraine, Europe, and the U.S. in Miami ended without a breakthrough — media reports  UA.NEWS
articles.full_text:
Talks between representatives of Ukraine, the U.S., European countries, and NATO in Miami concluded on October 9—one day earlier than planned. There will be no second day of meetings. This was announced on October 10 by Alex Raufoglu, senior correspondent for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty in Washington, and U.S. Special Representative Steve Witkoff.
The 
meeting was scheduled to last two days—October 9 and 10. Participants discussed possible ways to de-escalate and end Russia’s war against Ukraine ahead of winter.
The U.S. described the talks as constructive. Steve Witkoff stated that the parties discussed Ukraine’s energy security, preparations for winter, grain exports, security guarantees, post-war reconstruction, and the prospects for Ukraine’s accession to the EU. According to him, the meeting helped identify topics for further discussion ahead of the U.S.’s next contacts with Russia.
No specific agreements regarding a ceasefire were reported. At the same time, the U.S. side announced that it would continue working on diplomatic proposals.
According to preliminary reports, the Ukrainian delegation was represented by the Head of the Office of the President, Kirill Budanov; Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council, Rustem Umerov; First Deputy Head of the Office of the President, Serhiy Kyslytsia; and Chairman of the “Servant of the People” parliamentary faction, Davyd Arakhamia. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner participated in the talks on behalf of the U.S. Representatives from European countries and NATO also joined the meetings.
As a reminder, the Ukrainian negotiating delegation arrived in the U.S. on October 9 to meet with American officials in preparation for upcoming trilateral talks between Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia.

articles.title: Euro holds gains above 1.1200 despite France’s bond turmoil - FXStreet
articles.summary: Euro holds gains above 1.1200 despite France’s bond turmoil  FXStreet
articles.full_text:
The EUR/USD pair recovers some lost ground to near 1.1215 during the early Asian trading hours on Monday. The US Dollar (USD) softens against the Euro (EUR) after weaker-than-expected US Consumer Sentiment data. European Central Bank (ECB) Vice President Boris Vujčić is set to speak later in the day.
US consumer sentiment deteriorated further in October as soarinf oil prices due to the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy, the University of Michigan's (UoM) Surveys of Consumers showed on Friday. The UoM Consumer Sentiment Index dropped to 46.3 in October from 48.1 in September. This reading came in below the market consensus of 47.6.
Additionally, UoM one-year inflation expectations climbed to 4.7% in October from 4.6% in the previous reading. Consumers' expectations for inflation over the next five years jumped to 3.5% percent from 3.4% in September. However, this data has cemented expectations for a 25 basis points (bps) Federal Reserve (Fed) rate hike at their upcoming meeting.
On the other hand, French debt turmoil could exert some selling pressure on the shared currency. French government bond yields have surged to multiyear highs in recent days, as the country’s mounting debt crisis fuels wider concerns about Europe’s strained public finances.
Traders will closely monitor Italy amid contentious new government spending plans. The Italian government is set to introduce a budget encompassing recently approved allocations to defense and energy, which are expected to increase the country’s budget deficit over the next two years and push its debt-to-GDP ratio toward the highest level in Europe, according to CNBC.
Euro steadies as Eurozone resilience offsets rising China trade risks
Analysts at MUFG argue that, despite recent Euro weakness, they “continue to see evidence of economic resilience in Europe that could help stabilise the euro at these lower levels.” They point to Germany, where “the Economy Ministry… revised up its GDP growth projection from 0.5% and 0.9% for this year and next to 1.3% and 1.1% respectively.” Growth had previously been downgraded in response to the war, but MUFG notes that “the new estimate for this year is above the 1.0% estimate at the start of the year underlining the level of resilience.”
At the same time, the bank highlights mounting trade frictions with China as a potential headwind for the single currency. MUFG flags “speculation that Europe is soon to respond with agreeing to a more flexible trade policy mechanism that would allow for easier implementation to counter against huge imports to Europe from China,” adding that “an import cap could be agreed as well as additional tariffs that could see trade tensions rise and prompt retaliation from China.” The bank warns that “these talks could be the final opportunity to avoid increased tensions,” and cautions that “an escalation into grater trade conflict could be another EUR negative factor.”
On the currency side, MUFG observes that “this mounting pressure looks to be encouraging China too allow renewed gains.” They note that “recent PBoC fixing in USD/CNY indicate a desire to keep CNY on a strengthening path despite the broader gains for the dollar,” with “EUR/CNY… 10% lower from the January high” and “near-term scope for further declines.” The bank adds that “the continued CNY strength is helping isolate Asian currencies from the broader dollar gain,” pointing out that “while the DXY has advanced 3.3% from the September low, the dollar against a basket of Asia FX is just 0.7% higher.”
Moulin pins Eurozone inflation on energy as geopolitical shock deepens

By stressing that inflation is “clearly 100% energy” and that second-round effects are not visible, the speech leans mildly dovish on the underlying inflation dynamic, even as Moulin acknowledges an inflationary shock.
At the same time, the warning that the geopolitical shock is transmitting into a financial shock, while Euro area growth remains “quite resilient,” keeps the door open for the ECB to maintain a cautious policy stance. For the Euro, this mix of energy-driven inflation and resilience in activity suggests limited immediate hawkish escalation, but it reduces the scope for aggressive easing expectations in the near term.

Euro FAQs
The Euro is the currency for the 20 European Union countries that belong to the Eurozone. It is the second most heavily traded currency in the world behind the US Dollar. In 2022, it accounted for 31% of all foreign exchange transactions, with an average daily turnover of over $2.2 trillion a day. EUR/USD is the most heavily traded currency pair in the world, accounting for an estimated 30% off all transactions, followed by EUR/JPY (4%), EUR/GBP (3%) and EUR/AUD (2%).
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy. The ECB’s primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means either controlling inflation or stimulating growth. Its primary tool is the raising or lowering of interest rates. Relatively high interest rates – or the expectation of higher rates – will usually benefit the Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
Eurozone inflation data, measured by the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), is an important econometric for the Euro. If inflation rises more than expected, especially if above the ECB’s 2% target, it obliges the ECB to raise interest rates to bring it back under control. Relatively high interest rates compared to its counterparts will usually benefit the Euro, as it makes the region more attractive as a place for global investors to park their money.
Data releases gauge the health of the economy and can impact on the Euro. Indicators such as GDP, Manufacturing and Services PMIs, employment, and consumer sentiment surveys can all influence the direction of the single currency. A strong economy is good for the Euro. Not only does it attract more foreign investment but it may encourage the ECB to put up interest rates, which will directly strengthen the Euro. Otherwise, if economic data is weak, the Euro is likely to fall. Economic data for the four largest economies in the euro area (Germany, France, Italy and Spain) are especially significant, as they account for 75% of the Eurozone’s economy.
Another significant data release for the Euro is the Trade Balance. This indicator measures the difference between what a country earns from its exports and what it spends on imports over a given period. If a country produces highly sought after exports then its currency will gain in value purely from the extra demand created from foreign buyers seeking to purchase these goods. Therefore, a positive net Trade Balance strengthens a currency and vice versa for a negative balance.

Yandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on the Russian tech giant's sites this week.
The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users.
Earlier this week, Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its services after two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues in its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion.
Kyiv said it was targeting places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex.
Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market - a deal that has drawn criticism from Europe and sparked a diplomatic row with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity.
The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices.
The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.
On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed.
Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad.

articles.full_text:
The carmaker behind one of Britain’s most popular electric vehicles (EVs) has urged ministers to scale back “delusional” net zero targets amid fears they risk backfiring.
Adam Wood, the boss of Renault UK, insisted the French automotive giant supported the green transition and pointed to booming sales of the Renault 5 electric hatchback as proof that consumers would buy affordable cars.
However, he warned that the trajectory of the Government’s zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate was so steep that it was becoming “unsustainable” and could force manufacturers to scale back investment in EV technologies.
Speaking at the company’s office in north-west London, Mr Wood told The Telegraph: “For us, the debate is not the destination – we are absolutely convinced the destination is 100pc electric.
“The debate is about the speed at which we get there.
“But we shouldn’t be complacent or delusional that we have something today that is absolutely aligned with the ZEV mandate because we don’t.”
Mr Wood said consumer demand had “not kept pace with the ZEV mandate” and was being propped up by “unsustainable levels” of discounting by manufacturers.
He added: “The trajectory needs to be sustainable for the industry at a time when, let’s not forget, manufacturers are having to invest more than ever in the next generation of technology to make that transition happen.
“Anything that puts in jeopardy that investment – and the certainty that the automotive industry needs more than ever – is unhelpful.”
Ministers are reviewing the ZEV mandate following intense lobbying by carmakers, who say they are struggling to keep up.
Renault’s call to relax the rules will sound alarm bells in Whitehall because the company is one of the few that has managed to stay ahead of the targets.
This year’s headline requirement is for 33pc of cars sold to be electric.
Mr Wood said the French manufacturer’s sales are “approaching 50pc” thanks to the success of the revamped Renault 5. That compares with an overall market share of 26pc for electric cars so far this year.

articles.title: Something is rotten in the state of Germany - The Telegraph
articles.summary: Something is rotten in the state of Germany  The Telegraph‘Stab to the heart’: arrest of German ex-spymaster sparks calls for reform  The GuardianAn explosive allegation rocks Germany’s spy agency  The EconomistArrested German spy chief lashed out at his old agency over allegations he spied for Russia  POLITICO.euThe fall of Germany’s ex-spymaster  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
“The poison of betrayal is by no means as rare as we like to think of it. It’s not a nice part of our existence but it’s an entirely predictable one.”
I had good reason in recent days to remember this cynical observation on human nature and espionage as an extraordinary scandal rocked Germany and its allies.
My spy-philosopher was Markus Wolf, who had spent four decades at the helm of East Germany’s feared foreign intelligence services, earning himself the nickname “the man without a face” – which would be the title of our book.
It was the early 1990s and we were working many long days and evenings at his dacha, near an elite government colony outside East Berlin.
My assignment, as a journalist who had covered East Germany, was from US publisher Random House – to get his memoirs on track and ask him tough questions.
Over his ritual afternoon coffee and cigarette, Wolf continued his theme of betrayal. There was, he said “a class of treason that is particularly intensely felt and you do not forget – and that is a traitor inside one’s own secret service”.
“Someone you know well, who gives information to another one. This sort of betrayal is poison for every intelligence service – and the vaccines we have against it often have limited effects.”
His words reverberated this week after the bombshell revelation that August Hanning, the head of Germany intelligence from 1998 to 2005, has been arrested on a string of espionage and treason charges.
I found myself imagining what Wolf, who died aged 83 in 2006, would have made of it all, at a time of extraordinary vulnerability in Nato and threats inside Germany and the UK from Russian, Chinese and Iranian hostile operations.
The bigger the revelation, the more poker-faced the veteran spy-runner tended to be.
“Well, that’s a hammer” was often his droll German phrase when discussing some truly extraordinary incident adding secrets and espionage.
Hanning’s arrest has come as a sledgehammer to the BND, Germany’s counterpart to MI6. He is accused of paying Manfred Dankesreiter, his former chief of staff, to furnish him with more than 2,000 classified documents over 12 years, starting in 2010.
Hanning, now 80, allegedly intended to use the information to prepare briefing documents for Azerbaijan. Some of the information is believed to have covered Iran’s nuclear programme.
Hanning also reportedly had repeated contact with Wang Jianzheng, who had been stationed in Berlin as a military attaché.
He has denied treason and investigations continue. But no one is seriously denying that this is a vastly damaging moment for the BND.

articles.title: ‘A life-or-death race’: the volunteers protecting Kyiv’s skies from new jet-powered drones - The Guardian
articles.summary: ‘A life-or-death race’: the volunteers protecting Kyiv’s skies from new jet-powered drones  The GuardianDrone attack stops Russian government planes landing in Moscow  The TelegraphRussia is building jet drones that fly 800 kilometers per hour, and Ukraine says it is already working on how to stop next generation  Euromaidan PressMysterious Balloons and Drones Trigger Shutdown of All Four Moscow Airports  UNITED24 MediaUkraine’s air defenses down 94 of 116...
articles.full_text:
Several hours into Kyiv’s nightly curfew, much of the capital lay dark and quiet. High above, on the roof of a grey tower block on the city’s outskirts, a small group of men in uniform stood beside two heavy machine guns, scanning the horizon. Soon, a drone appeared.
Once, its unmistakable buzz would have sent the men scrambling towards their weapons. Now, the air defence unit will check speed and altitude on a monitor before taking a decision.

This one flew too high and too fast. It was one of Russia’s new jet-powered attack drones, a weapon that has transformed the battle for the skies over Kyiv in just a few months.
“They’re so fast, it’s extremely difficult to hit them. Our weapons simply can’t reach them. Often, we can hear them but can’t see them. It drives us crazy,” said the group’s commander, who goes by the call sign Sensei, looking over the city’s skyline.
Over three days and nights, the Guardian accompanied Mriya, Kyiv’s largest volunteer air-defence formation, across its network of outposts around the capital, from high-rise rooftops to truck-mounted machine gun positions in deserted fields on the city’s outskirts.
Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine has relied on unpaid volunteers, often armed with Soviet-era weapons, as one layer of the air-defence network protecting its cities, homes and families.
For years, they proved remarkably effective, emerging as a key part of the response to the Iranian-designed Shahed drones, which Russia calls Geran-2 and began launching en masse in late 2022.
“We live a double life. During the day, I deal with paperwork. At night, I shoot down drones,” said Oleksandr, a lawyer, standing beside his truck-mounted machine gun in a field outside Kyiv. “It’s a strange duality. With time you get used to it.”
But warfare in Ukraine evolves at extraordinary speed and units such as Mriya are struggling to keep up.
Since the summer, Russia has increasingly deployed jet-powered drones that crews say can travel at about 600km/h (373mph), much faster than the original propeller-driven Shaheds, and reach altitudes of up to 10km (6 miles), far beyond the range of the volunteers’ guns.
Ukraine’s interception rate for the new drones is between 50% and 60%.
“In 2023 and 2024, we were shooting them down in batches,” Artem, a 63-year-old military veteran, said proudly. On a good night, he added, a single crew could bring down three or four Shaheds.
Now, his unit had managed to shoot down just one jet drone after it slowed enough to come within range of their guns. “There’s this feeling of helplessness,” he added.
The problem, Artem explained, was that the guns’ sights were designed for slower targets. Jet drones fly so fast that gunners must aim beyond the sight to hit them. “The Shahed no longer fits inside our aiming grid,” he said.
Ukraine’s air defences operate as a layered system, with different weapons matched to different threats. Volunteer machine gun teams work alongside interceptor drones to hunt slower, low-flying Shaheds. More sophisticated weapons, including the country’s scarce US-made Patriot batteries, are needed against cruise and ballistic missiles.
For now, the main answer to the jet drones has been fighter aircraft, including F-16s, which are expensive to fly and put their pilots at risk.
Russia’s introduction of new drones came at an especially acute moment for Ukraine. With its ground offensive making slow progress, Russia has sharply intensified its air campaign, striking Kyiv almost daily in an effort to make the capital unlivable as winter approaches.
In the last week, jet-powered drones have repeatedly struck bridges across the Dnipro in Kyiv, prompting restrictions on several of the city’s main crossings. Russia launched another large-scale bombardment across Ukraine on Wednesday, firing dozens of missiles alongside drones and causing fresh disruption to electricity and water supplies in the capital.
The attacks have upended daily life in a city that, for much of the war, was considered relatively safe compared with those nearer the front. Anti-drone netting, long a familiar sight in frontline towns, has begun to appear around Kyiv, and during the heaviest attacks some people have taken to sleeping in metro stations.
Moscow has also begun sending waves of jet drones throughout the day, a break with years of assaults taking place mostly overnight.
“Every hour, two or three come in,” said Oleksandr, the lawyer, who joined Mriya early last year. His mobile group once deployed from base as drones approached the city, but now spends hours at a time waiting in fields.
“They’re fast and they keep our groups constantly moving. Some days, it feels like Russia has an endless supply of them,” he shrugged.
Mriya’s volunteers are something of a mirror of Kyiv. The crews that the Guardian accompanied included in their ranks an advertising creative director, a man who repairs intercoms, a hand-to-hand combat coach and the former head of a design institute.
The military supplies the units with heavy machine guns, including American-made Browning M2s and Soviet-era DShKs, both designed before the second world war. But the volunteers pay for their own vehicles, fuel and other equipment.
What united them, they said, was that the stakes felt close to home. “If we let a drone through, that means it flies to the city and can kill our families,” said Ivan, a university professor in Kyiv.
Ivan joined the unit after a Shahed struck the courtyard of his home about a year and a half ago. “It badly frightened my family and destroyed my property,” he said. “So I had a personal score to settle as well. I have two children. The more of this filth that is destroyed on the approach to Kyiv, the lower the chance that my children will be hurt.”
When a shift runs into the morning, he teaches his class online from the position, on his phone. Others described volunteering as a way of reclaiming a measure of agency over a war that has left millions of Ukrainians feeling powerless.
“In the city you can’t do anything. People sit in basements, bomb shelters or apartments and wait: will you be lucky or not, will it hit or not?” Oleksandr said. Out on the position, he said, there was at least a chance of shooting one down.
Help, though, may be on its way. Back in the field, Artem pulled out a tablet showing a live map of drones over Ukraine.
Among the moving icons were ones the volunteers have begun to see more often: Ukraine’s new generation of high-speed interceptor drones, designed to hunt down their Russian counterparts.
He pointed to two Ukrainian interceptors travelling at more than 600km/h. Moments later, each brought down a Russian drone and disappeared from the screen.
Across the country, the Ukrainian government and private defence companies have been thrown into a race to build jet-powered interceptors that can match Russia’s latest drones.
“We have to admit that we were caught sleeping by these jet-powered Shaheds,” said Stanislav Hryshyn, a co-founder of General Cherry, one of Ukraine’s largest drone manufacturers, which is developing the new interceptors.
The biggest obstacle, he said, was a shortage of the small jet engines that power them, which Russia sources in bulk from China. Neither Ukraine nor Europe, Hryshyn said, had built the industrial capacity to make them in the quantities required.
Hryshyn estimated it would take three to four months before Ukraine could produce enough interceptors to match Russia’s jet drones.
Even if Ukraine fields thousands of new interceptors in the coming months, any advantage may prove short-lived. Russia has repeatedly adapted its drones, changing their speed, altitude and flight paths in response to Ukrainian defences, and Hryshyn said each new countermeasure invited another innovation.
“It’s a constant race over who gets there first,” Hryshyn said. “A life-or-death race.”

articles.title: City of London hits out at Andy Burnham’s plan to scrap non-compete clauses - Financial Times
articles.summary: City of London hits out at Andy Burnham’s plan to scrap non-compete clauses  Financial TimesBurnham promises to curb non-compete rules in job contracts  BBCUK plans to announce ban on workers’ non-compete clauses in push for growth  POLITICO.euNotice and non-compete periods - what's standard for UK startups?  SeedLegalsIf Britain loves its tech talent, it must set it free  The Observer
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Hedge funds and banks have hit out at Andy Burnham’s plan to end the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts, warning the proposal risks “throwing the baby out with the bathwater” and could disadvantage UK firms.
The prime minister said on Friday that the government would “legislate to make sure that non-compete clauses will no longer be a barrier to hiring for our most promising start-ups and scaling firms”.
Burnham’s plan to restrict non-compete clauses, which constrain a worker’s ability to work for a competitor for a period of time after leaving their current employer, has been welcomed by tech groups. But his promise triggered a swift backlash in the City of London.
“Our members are very disappointed by this proposal,” said John Godfrey, a managing director at TheCityUK, which represents some of the largest UK financial groups. “They feel it will potentially damage the competitiveness of UK financial and professional services.”
Many companies in the City of London, including hedge funds, investment banks and wealth managers, rely on non-compete agreements to try to stop their star traders, money managers and dealmakers being poached by rivals.
Burnham said the practice was “a drag on innovation”, adding: “We need our innovators to be able to move freely between companies and start their own without constraint.”
But supporters of non-compete clauses say they are needed to protect intellectual property, client relationships and investment in training and development of key staff.
“The UK government risks throwing the baby out with the bathwater in its efforts to support the tech sector,” said Jiří Król at the Alternative Investment Management Association, which represents hedge funds and private equity groups.
At top hedge funds, non-compete clauses often mean portfolio managers have to sit out of the market for as long as 18 months to two years before they can join a rival, while an analyst might have to wait a year.
Jillien Flores, at the Managed Funds Association, which represents most of the world’s biggest hedge funds, said: “Non-compete agreements are vital tools for protecting the proprietary investment strategies that underpin the alternative asset management industry.”
Godfrey at TheCityUK said companies could respond to a ban on non-compete clauses by making staff notice periods longer. He also warned that any changes should apply only to new contracts.
A review into non-competes was launched last year by then prime minister Sir Keir Starmer, setting out options ranging from an outright ban to placing a time limit — for example of three months — on the arrangements.
The founders of some leading UK tech start-ups last month called on ministers to limit the use of non-compete clauses and extended notice periods, arguing they hampered British businesses’ ability to compete with Silicon Valley.
Companies in California are banned from using non-compete clauses. The US Federal Trade Commission voted for a nationwide ban in 2024, but it backed down after the move was challenged by businesses in a Texas court.
The UK government said: “We want the UK to be the best place for firms to start, scale, list and stay, and ensuring non-compete clauses aren’t a barrier to hiring the best talent is a key way to make sure these innovative businesses aren’t held back.”
“Backing the financial sector will be equally critical for growth, which is why we’re already unlocking billions of pounds of private capital through landmark pension reforms and overhauling listing rules, all to make the sector as competitive and streamlined as possible,” it added.
Officials aim to set out more detail of the reform plans alongside this month’s Budget. They want to help fast-growing sectors such as AI recruit skilled people more easily, believing there are other ways companies can protect intellectual property, such as trade secrets laws and confidentiality clauses in contracts.
“Hiring faster means British start-ups and scale-ups can grow faster,” said Dom Hallas at the Startup Coalition. “By addressing these barriers the prime minister can materially impact the trajectory of the UK tech ecosystem and with it, UK growth.”
However, UK industry groups have warned it could create an unnecessary impediment for British companies to ban non-compete clauses, which are included in the contracts of about 5mn British employees — typically with a duration of about six months.
“Many businesses rely on non-competes to protect commercially sensitive information and support investment in people and new ideas,” said Matthew Percival, a director at the CBI business lobby group. “We have not seen compelling evidence that non-compete clauses are a drag on innovation or a material hindrance on labour market mobility.”

articles.title: China moves to stave off wider EU trade war with hybrid deal - The Business Times
articles.summary: China moves to stave off wider EU trade war with hybrid deal  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
Both agree to slash millions of hybrid car exports, with the bloc said to be planning to curb imports
WITH an agreement to curb exports of hybrid vehicles to the EU, China is betting it can sidestep harsher restrictions from the 27-member bloc with a gesture that has little immediate prospect of reshaping the overall trade relationship.
Talks between China and the EU ended late on Friday (Oct 9) with a 16-point consensus spanning trade and investment, export controls and intellectual property rights.
The EU said China agreed to slash millions of hybrid car exports, with people familiar with discussions saying the bloc intends to use safeguard measures to curb imports.
EU leaders meet on Thursday to decide whether to adopt a more forceful response to the surge in Chinese exports, which threaten to hollow out European manufacturing industries and decimate millions of jobs.
Germany and France last week called for stronger tools – including an instrument that could cut off China from the bloc’s massive single market – to defend sectors hit by surging subsidised Chinese imports.
The agreement on Friday buys time for further negotiations, with the two sides planning for more talks in January and March, said Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at research firm Trivium China.
He called it a strategic win for China, saying in a research note that “Beijing has played a blinder”.
“In exchange for reviews, dialogue, and ‘understandings’, it has conceded little on the structural drivers of the EU’s massive trade deficit,” he wrote.
“Beyond vehicles and modest tariff relief, nothing in the 16-point agreement suggests a significant rewiring of China’s trading terms with the EU.”
EU leaders are seeking ways to stop China from flooding the continent with goods that have led to a trade deficit now exceeding 1 billion euros (US$1.1 billion) a day.
Weak consumption at home has left China increasingly reliant on a world-beating manufacturing sector and overseas demand to support its sluggish domestic economy.
China’s Ministry of Commerce on Friday said the two sides reaffirmed their commitment as key trading partners to properly manage differences under World Trade Organization (WTO) rules.
They also agreed to maintain stable bilateral economic and trade ties while making them “more balanced”.
Friday’s joint statement said the two sides had reached an “understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles in a WTO compliant manner”.
Chinese hybrid car sales have escalated in part because they escaped the EU’s 2024 tariffs on EVs.
In August, Chinese car brands accounted for about a quarter of European hybrid sales.
Safeguard measures planned by the EU typically take the form of tariff-rate quotas, which apply a levy on imports above a certain volume to curb excess flows.
That would comply with WTO rules – something both China and the EU have said is a requirement.
EU ambassadors briefed by trade chief Maros Sefcovic on Sunday broadly welcomed the result while stressing that they viewed it as just the beginning of the process to rebalance the trade relationship, according to people familiar with the talks, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The goal is for the EU safeguard measures to apply from Dec 1.
Chinese carmakers like Chery Automobile have massively stepped up vehicle shipments to the EU in response to a slump in their home market, exacerbating a deceleration plaguing European peers, which are among the worst-performing globally.
Mercedes-Benz Group car sales dropped by 8 per cent in the third quarter, while Volkswagen in September slashed its profit forecast following a similar warning from BMW in June.
Renault chief executive officer Francois Provost called the deal with China a “major milestone” that will help foster a future for Europe’s automotive industry.
He was among business leaders who met with Sefcovic ahead of his trip to China for the talks.
“I had urged him to seek an agreement quickly,” Provost said in an interview on Sunday.
“Without one, we would be looking at a trade war with China, which would be a lose-lose situation for everyone.”
The timing of the EU-China agreement “indicates that China is keen to ease tensions” before the bloc’s leaders meet, said Henry Gao, a law professor at Singapore Management University.
“Given its ongoing trade frictions with the United States, Beijing is unlikely to want a simultaneous escalation with Europe.”
“If the EU insists on strictly WTO-consistent approaches, such measures may not be particularly effective in addressing the surge of Chinese exports, as past cases have demonstrated,” Gao added.
“WTO-compliant trade remedies can provide some relief, but they are often limited in scope and may not significantly alter broader trade flows.”
France and Germany have called on the EU to investigate whether subsidised imports are harming sectors like chemicals and plastics – probes that could produce more tariffs.
The proposal was seen as a pressure tactic targeting Beijing, putting Germany’s weight behind forceful moves it had previously opposed.
“It has taken a tremendous amount of political capital for European officials to get this far on autos, and it’s not clear that the approach could be easily copy-pasted to other industries,” said Christopher Beddor, deputy China research director at Gavekal Dragonomics.
Beijing has preemptively warned the EU against adopting what it called protectionist measures.
China’s dominance of critical rare earth supplies – leverage it has already wielded in trade negotiations with the US – gives Beijing a powerful deterrent as Europe simultaneously tries to curb Chinese imports and secure the materials its factories need.
“Sweeping trade barriers and tariffs would probably incur retaliation from Beijing, and Chinese officials have the nuclear option of threatening to restrict rare-earths exports,” Beddor said.
“But at this stage, they seem more inclined to cut a deal.” BLOOMBERG

articles.full_text:
China and the European Union have reached a preliminary agreement to limit the export of Chinese hybrid vehicles to the European market. Beijing hopes this will help it avoid tougher trade restrictions from the EU. Bloomberg reports, according to UNN.
Details
The negotiations concluded with an agreement on 16 points covering trade, investment, export controls, and intellectual property protection. One of the key outcomes was China’s agreement to reduce supplies of hybrid vehicles to Europe.
According to Bloomberg, the European Union is preparing safeguard measures against excessive imports. In particular, it is considering tariff quotas that would impose additional duties on vehicles once the established supply volume is exceeded.
Why the EU wants to limit Chinese cars
Chinese manufacturers are actively expanding their presence in Europe, in part because hybrid vehicles were not subject to the duties imposed by the EU on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024. In August, Chinese brands accounted for about a quarter of European hybrid sales.

French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market.
The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs.
As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028.
As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors.
Farmers’ favourite
Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow".
The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around.
The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs.
Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair.
The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists.
Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000.
The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor.
The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses".
By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road.
VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success.
BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades.
Retro-nostalgia
But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers.
Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well.
VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta.
Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense.
"It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect."
Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands.
"Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data.
In this hostile business environment, heritage and nostalgia could prove to be powerful weapons for more established brands, thinks automotive researcher and author Dr Paul Nieuwenhuis.
"In a world where a wave of credible decent quality Chinese EVs are hitting Europe, linking European designs back to their history while using the latest powertrain technology is something the Chinese cannot do," he says.
"The Chinese can establish new design trends, but there is limited history there."
But Leggett thinks Citroen will need more than a heady whiff of nostalgia to turn its new car into a best-seller.
"A reimagined Citroën 2CV should give a big nod to its ancestor - especially on price and design simplicity as well as visual cues," he says.
"But it also needs to be a credible modern electric car in terms of functionality and features, with widespread appeal."

articles.title: EU and China set out 16 outcomes from trade consultations, with key terms still to come - London Daily News
articles.summary: EU and China set out 16 outcomes from trade consultations, with key terms still to come  London Daily News
articles.full_text:
The European Union and China have outlined 16 areas of agreement after two days of trade and investment consultations in Beijing on 8 and 9 October. The outcomes span trade balance, export controls, intellectual property and reform of the World Trade Organization. They also set out further work on tariffs, hybrid-vehicle trade, electric-vehicle price undertakings and foreign-subsidy rules.
The announcement is a framework for continued discussions, not a completed package of binding trade agreements. Both sides said work would continue through technical and ministerial channels, with a ministerial video meeting planned for January 2027 and the next formal consultation meeting scheduled for March. The two governments described the talks as a way to manage differences and keep economic ties stable while seeking a more balanced relationship.
Several practical questions remain open
The parties said they would keep exploring possible tariff reductions on certain goods within World Trade Organization rules. They did not publish a comprehensive list of products, rates or implementation dates in the available public account. That means the announcement signals a negotiating direction rather than a tariff change businesses can apply immediately.
On hybrid vehicles, the sides reported an understanding on trade that they said would be consistent with WTO rules. They did not provide public operational detail on how it would work. It should not be confused with a settled arrangement on battery-electric vehicles: the separate electric-vehicle anti-subsidy case remains subject to procedures concerning company-specific price undertakings and reviews. These undertakings are an alternative issue being considered within that trade-remedy process, not a statement that existing measures have already been removed.
The consultations also opened a technical dialogue on the EU Foreign Subsidies Regulation. That regulation gives the EU a framework to examine distortions linked to foreign financial contributions, including in some market and public-procurement situations. Agreement to discuss its operation does not amount to an exemption or a finding about any particular company.
Export licensing and market access
Export controls were another prominent area. China said it would continue facilitating EU-bound applications for rare-earth and permanent-magnet exports through a green-channel process. The EU, for its part, said it would work with member states to help resolve priority licensing cases for exports to China in the dual-use sector—goods or technology with both civilian and potential military applications.
The public summaries describe cooperation and case handling, rather than a general removal of licensing requirements. Companies dependent on these materials or controlled goods will still need to follow the applicable licensing rules. The sides also committed to further communication on export-control policies and to dialogue on transparency around control listings and procedures.
Other subjects in the 16-point list include intellectual-property protection, investment cooperation and WTO reform. The parties said work on intellectual-property issues would continue, including efforts to improve fairness, transparency and predictability. Their WTO commitment was to deepen communication and engage in the reform process; no specific reform text or timetable was announced.
A process rather than a final settlement
The next steps are important because many of the headline outcomes remain dependent on follow-up by officials, regulators, companies or EU member states. A consultation mechanism can keep disputes in negotiation and help clarify technical procedures, but it does not by itself settle the wider arguments over market access, subsidies, export restrictions or the balance of trade.
For now, the clearest immediate result is a shared agenda and a commitment to continue talks. The scheduled January ministerial contact and March meeting give the sides a route to test whether the stated understandings can be translated into specific, workable measures. Until further details are agreed and published, the 16 outcomes should be read as consultation results—not as proof that tariffs, licensing rules or electric-vehicle trade measures have already changed.

Marc Poskett, has vowed not to use a stocks and shares ISA again, after losing money while saving for his first home.
39-year-old Marc, from Middlesborough, North Yorkshire is “frustrated” about a change in the ISA rules from April, which will mean he can save less into his cash ISA.
An ISA is a special account where you never pay tax on the interest or gains you make. There are multiple different types of ISA but the most common are the cash ISA – which is a savings account – or a stocks and shares ISA – where you invest money.
Shorts
You can currently put £20,000 into an ISA each tax year and the money can be spread across each of these two forms in any way you wish.
From April 2027, that will change, and you will only be able to save £12,000 a year into a cash ISA, unless you are 65 or over.
The remaining £8,000 of your allowance will have to go into a stocks and shares ISA or the rarely used innovative finance ISA, but Marc says he won’t be using either of these.
He first opened a cash ISA in 2017 and saved £20,000 into it to buy his first home in 2024.
He’s now saving to buy a second home – a buy-to-let – but says he won’t be pushed to invest instead of using cash.
“I previously tried stocks and shares and lost money while I was saving for my first home. My approach come April 2027 will be trying to maximise my cash ISA allowance and put anything above the limit into a standard savings account to buy my second property,” he explained.
The housing support co-ordinator from Middlesborough, described the new rules as a “massive change” and will make him have to rethink his finances.
“It is going to make a hard process even more confusing because I am now going to have to spread my savings across more accounts,” Marc explained.
He’s currently using a cash ISA to purchase the buy-to-let property and has £8,000 saved in there.
Marc intends to max out his £20,000 ISA allowance before the rules change in April 2027.
He currently puts in £200 a month but will be increasing this to ensure he makes use of the full allowance.
Marc said he likes saving into a cash ISA because he really values the safety, steady interest and accessibility the product provides.
He added: “It doesn’t go up or down unlike stocks and shares, which gives me peace of mind for my shorter-term savings.”
Data from Nottingham Building Society found a quarter of cash ISA holders were now making contributions of more than £15,000 this year, with the average contributions rising 24 per cent since 2024.
The government introduced the changes to the ISA rules to encourage more people to invest, but Marc believes it will make buying a second home harder to reach.
“I understand that the government wants people to invest but my view is that you’ve worked hard for your money, so why should I have to put my money into something that I don’t want to understand or want to do?” he argues.
Brian Byrnes, head of personal finance at Moneybox said that the cash ISA cut would likely frustrate consumers rather than encourage them to start investing, as it will create more complexity.
He said: “It will also limit choice and prevent people from building up the financial confidence they need in order to start investing in the first place.”
But he did say that he believed more people should be investing, once they had an emergency fund of cash savings built up.
He added: “Historically, investments have outperformed cash savings over the long term. And even when you’ve been diligent and feel as though you’ve saved a substantial amount in cash, inflation silently erodes its purchasing power over time.”
The i Paper previously reported Andy Burnham’s Government will press ahead with reforms to the cash ISA in the spring – but a major bank has warned that it is still awaiting key details needed to implement the changes in time.
With less than seven months to go before the new rules take effect on 6 April, 2027, the finance industry is demanding clarity on how the change will work – with some calling for a delay.
