But the exhilaration soon turns to panic. With a thick black canopy of smoke creeping along the ceiling of the main corridor, they realise it’s time to go: “Come on, come on, there’s smoke everywhere. Fuck, I can’t see a thing!” They’re soon scarpering into the surrounding streets in broad daylight, the cameraman sipping his Capri-Sun as a column of smoke rises from the school, and police cars converge on the site.
The Marcel Pagnol arson was perhaps the most serious incident of a phenomenon that has swept the whole of France in recent years: comprehensive trashings of school premises that go well beyond isolated acts of vandalism. There were at least 15 cases in 2025; a similar number in 2024. The damage inflicted on at least 24 high schools across the country during this month’s student protests seem to some extent to fit this pattern – though these actions are fuelled by particular shared grievances, including dilapidated facilities and endemic staff shortages. Perhaps attacks on schools like Marcel Pagnol should have served as canaries in the coalmine for rising tension, resentment and nihilistic feeling among students towards the institutions supposedly there to guarantee their future. Such events crop up in other countries, but here they seem to fit a pattern of carnivalesque destruction – like the mass burning of cars during urban riots – that seems distinctively French. In a sense, trashings are the country’s equivalent of school shootings in America – though obviously far less deadly and generally perpetrated by groups, not loners.
To highlight a few: smashed computers and broken windows at Rabelais secondary school in Vitry-sur-Seine in March 2024, the fourth break-in in six months; graffiti of a swastika, an anarchist symbol and anti‑Rassemblement National (RN) slogans left behind by ideologically confused hooligans at André Malraux secondary school in Baignes-Sainte-Radegonde, near Bordeaux; “Foke les profs” (Fuck the teachers) scrawled amid the devastation at Jean Moulin primary school in Montgeron, on Paris’s southern edge; one primary school and two nursery schools laid waste to in 2025 in working-class neighbourhoods of the Provençal city of Arles.
In a strikingly large number of cases, it is primary schools that are attacked. When the perpetrators are caught, they are often children of early secondary-school age returning to wreak havoc. In many cases, they’re trashing the same schools in which their younger siblings are still taught. “My sister’s got school here tomorrow,” crows one of the intruders in the video from École Marcel Pagnol. On the one hand, there’s a festive misrule in such acts: the paint-lashed walls, the upturned shelves, the rainbow debris of playbricks strewn across play areas. On the other, there’s an aspect of psychological self-harm in play, akin to destroying the family home, that’s also visible in this month’s lycée attacks. It’s hard to square this beguiling clash of motives.
What’s clear is the impact on the surrounding community. Two years after the attack, on a humid June Monday morning, the final one before the summer holidays, pupils and parents are ambling up to Marcel Pagnol to start the school day. It’s situated in the suburb of Meyzieu, a relatively well-off and unremarkable commuter dormitory of Lyon set in the arable land that sprawls towards the city airport. The school’s cream, two-storey blocks have been restored to pristine condition – at a cost of €1.9m to the Meyzieu municipality (partly covered by insurance).
But the attack caused a real sense of violation. “I’m sad,” six-year-old Lino told reporters from TV station BFM right after the arson. “All my drawings burned.” And the feeling still lingers. “They set the school alight with a toxic product,” says Evan, a boy of eight or nine with thumbs inside his backpack strap. “There were flames.” Audrey Granger, a member of the parents’ association, points out the children had to process seeing their charred drawings on the walls, the burnt exercise books. She didn’t tell her daughter, who attended the nursery school next door, what had happened. “We wanted to leave her in her own little bubble,” she says.
“It was as if you left your office and someone said to you: you have no right to come back,” Juliane Fauriat, the headteacher, says. “You didn’t anticipate it, you have to leave everything behind, which is very difficult.” Her staff removed salvageable equipment in crates provided by the town hall; two traumatised teachers walked out with empty boxes from their entirely burnt-out classrooms.
The following academic year, Marcel Pagnol’s 240 pupils were housed in prefab annexes on an empty field opposite – a novelty for some of them. But with the canteen severely damaged, lunchtime had to be split between two other school sites: one a bus ride away for the younger children; another 15 minutes’ walk away for the older ones. “They had to do it in the heat of summer and in winter,” says Sabrina, a mum in a flowery dress lingering at the end of the school run. “Can you imagine? My daughter was crying sometimes – she was always running late.”
The two 13-year-old perpetrators – one of whom shows his face in the video and names the other – were caught almost immediately. They had no criminal record and were unknown to the police; one had an “irreproachable” academic record, says Sandrine Carroz, a coordinator with the municipality’s education services. The other was going through a “fragile period, where communication with his parents was complicated”. But there had been nothing to indicate he might erupt in this way. Sylvie Normand, the deputy mayor of Meyzieu, the area served by École Marcel Pagnol, says: “I think these were young people who dared each other to do something and who came up with a bad idea, which went through their heads without them thinking about the consequences.”
The online lynch mob assembled: “Give them another chance – they were just expressing their anger at having to retake year 3 for the fifth time” is one sarcastic comment under a news report posted on YouTube. Others hint at the societal and ethnic tensions inflaming French public life – heightened in Lyon, which is a centre of far-right activity: “Kick them out of the country, along with the parents who are taking our family allowances.” (Based on the name mentioned by one of the boys in the videos, and their slang, many commenters assumed they had immigrant origins; their identities as minors are of course protected by law.) Tiffany Joncour, the local RN candidate, was quickly on the scene to film a video declaring: “It’s time to stop these delinquents who act with impunity and spoil all our lives.”
The pair received four-month suspended sentences and were placed under special court supervision for 18 months. The municipality agreed with the two families to send their siblings to other schools. Over the road from École Marcel Pagnol, boulangerie worker Miriam is more circumspect than most: “It could have been my child – because you never know, especially with the influence of social networks these days. I hope it knocks some sense into them. And their families, too, because they have to take some responsibility.”
As the Marcel Pagnol perpetrators are minors, it’s impossible to ask them the crucial question: what led them to break down the front door on that day? But perhaps it’s possible to pursue a second one: what do these messy tremors from the teenage subconscious collectively say about French society?
‘They think it’s not worthy of respect – so they trash it.” Outside Louise-Michel primary school in Arles earlier this year in March, parent Etienne Becker suggests it was a fundamental disdain for national institutions that led four youths, aged between 11 and 13, to break and enter and do approximately €30,000 worth of damage there in July 2025. He’s dropping his six-year-old son off at a squat, tan complex with a barracks-like air. Louise‑Michel is on the edge of Griffeuille, a marginalised neighbourhood dominated by hal‑rendered blocks of public housing in which 57% live below the poverty line.
The values of the French state – “Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité” – are displayed on insignia outside almost all the country’s schools (as Becker points out, they are curiously absent at Louise-Michel). It’s in places like Griffeuille where it’s easiest to assume that school trashings may be a form of aggression, conscious or not, towards how these lofty ideals translate in practice. Éric Debarbieux, a veteran researcher who formerly directed the International Observatory of Violence in School and has advised the French government, corroborates this, suggesting that for the attackers, “it’s a way of saying: schools don’t keep their promises. The values displayed aren’t the same as the values in reality.”

articles.title: House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal - Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.summary: House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal  Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON -- Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick plans to force a House vote on legislation blocking Russian oil purchases, challenging President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports as lawmakers warn the move could help finance Moscow's war against Ukraine.
Fitzpatrick (Republican-Pennsylvania), co-chair of the House Ukraine Caucus, announced on October 10 that he would introduce the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.
“We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil,” Fitzpatrick wrote on X. “It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly.”
Representative Don Bacon (Republican-Nebraska) has agreed to co-sponsor the bill. A Democratic sponsor had not been identified.
A discharge petition can force a House vote without approval from the relevant committee or House leadership if it secures 218 signatures.
The effort faces time constraints: Congress is not scheduled to resume voting for several weeks, and the current congressional term ends in January. Any bill would also need Senate approval and could face White House opposition.
Fitzpatrick invoked former President Ronald Reagan's approach to confronting Moscow and reaffirmed congressional support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Trump has again criticized.
“Russia illegally invaded Ukraine. Russia is squarely to blame,” Fitzpatrick wrote, adding that Congress and the American people stood behind Zelenskyy “until Ukrainian victory is achieved.”
Republicans Question Sanctions Reversal
The proposed legislation reflects concern among some Republicans that easing Russian energy restrictions could undermine pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Representative Michael McCaul (Republican-Texas), the former chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, warned that lifting sanctions could “fund the Kremlin's war machine -- emboldening more violence and destruction.”
He cited the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed in September. The law authorizes the president, under specified conditions, to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian energy. McCaul said it gave Trump leverage over Russia and China to help secure a negotiated end to the war.
Senator Lisa Murkowski (Republican-Alaska) urged Trump to use those authorities instead of allowing Russia to earn more from diesel exports.
“We can discuss Russia's return to global energy markets once the war is over, but in the meantime, we need to cut off everything fueling it,” she wrote on social media.
Democrats Cite Existing Oil Ban
Democrats and former officials have also pointed to the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which prohibits Russian oil imports into the United States unless the president certifies that Russia has met specified conditions, including withdrawing from Ukraine, recognizing Ukrainian sovereignty and posing no threat to NATO.
The law passed the Senate 100-0 and the House 413-9 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Former Representative Tom Malinowski, also a former top State Department official, urged Democratic leaders to use the law's expedited procedures to challenge the administration's decision.
“Under this law, House and Senate Democratic leaders can introduce a ‘Joint Resolution of Disapproval’ to prevent the purchase of Russian oil, which Congress then has to vote on in an expedited manner,” Malinowski wrote on social media.
“Schumer and Jeffries should do so ASAP,” he added, referring to Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries.
Whether the 2022 law applies to the latest arrangement remains a key question as the administration's temporary authorization for Russian diesel exports faces scrutiny.
Advocates Warn Of Damage To Sanctions
Daniel Balson, advocacy director at Razom for Ukraine, told RFE/RL that Trump's decision undermined the purpose of the sanctions legislation passed weeks earlier.
“Three weeks ago, Congress passed the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. This bill was designed to force other countries to lower their Russian energy dependence. President Trump's recent decision just increased our own,” Balson said.
He urged lawmakers to challenge the move to protect Ukraine and the credibility of congressional action. Although he had not seen Fitzpatrick's bill, Balson said pro-Ukraine advocates would pursue “any and all legislative avenues” to oppose the decision.
Senator Angus King, an independent from Maine who generally votes with Democrats, said in a statement that the agreement would offer little relief to American consumers while benefiting Russia.
Citing administration figures, King said the deal covered 300,000 tons of diesel for October and 500,000 tons for November -- roughly equivalent to a day's diesel consumption in the United States.
“This so-called deal with Russia will do little for America and much for Vladimir Putin as he seeks to sustain his murderous campaign on Ukraine,” King said. He called the agreement “a fraud.”
Trump Again Calls For Zelenskyy To Be Replaced
Trump on October 10 renewed his attacks on Zelenskyy, saying Ukraine should hold an election and replace its president with a leader willing to reach an agreement with Russia.
“Well, I think he should have an election. And he could have settled this thing many times,” Trump told reporters.
Earlier, Trump had said Ukraine should “get a new leader who can make a deal.” He also demanded that Kyiv “damn well stop” attacking Russian oil refineries, which Ukraine has targeted to disrupt Moscow's war economy and fuel supplies.
Trump blamed Zelenskyy for failing to secure a settlement, a claim at odds with Kyiv’s position that any agreement must protect Ukraine’s sovereignty and with lawmakers’ calls to maintain pressure on Moscow. Trump also portrayed Putin as eager for peace and praised the release of Russian oil onto global markets.
“It surely looks bad. The president has always had a moral blindness when it comes to Putin. Propping up Russia's war economy is terrible,” Bacon told RFE/RL.
Trump's remarks came hours after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhya.
Zelenskyy has said elections cannot be held under martial law and amid the security risks created by Russia's invasion. Ukrainian officials have also cited the need to ensure soldiers and displaced citizens can participate in a credible vote.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha issued a statement late on October 10 backing the Ukrainian president.
Zelenskyy "leads our nation in a time of war -- a war for independence, freedom, and dignity. He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support," Sybiha wrote on X.
EU Rejects Easing Pressure On Russia
European officials criticized the diesel agreement, warning that additional Russian energy revenue could help sustain the war.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russian strikes had killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians over the past two days and that Moscow had intensified hybrid attacks against EU member states and NATO allies.
“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't,” Kallas said, adding that EU foreign ministers planned to announce a major new round of sanctions on October 12 targeting people and organizations supporting Moscow's war effort.
Germany also reaffirmed its commitment to existing sanctions and said it would work with European partners on further measures.
A spokesman for Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Berlin stood by its restrictions, while government spokesman Stefan Kornelius reiterated support for Ukraine. Economics Minister Katherina Reiche also backed the EU sanctions packages.
Germany's Fuels and Energy Trade Association said it did not expect the agreement to have a major effect on petrol-station prices.

articles.title: Trump: Germany was two days away from total collapse ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - World - Fakti.bg
articles.summary: Trump: Germany was two days away from total collapse ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - World  Fakti.bg
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump said that Germany was “just two days away from extinction“ after betting on green energy. He made the statement at an election rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, where he criticized policies for the development of wind and solar energy.
“We don't need green energy. Show me a country that uses green energy, and I'll tell you it's on the verge of bankruptcy. You know, Germany already tried it and they were only two days away from extinction“, Trump said, quoted in a Fox News video.
The US president did not provide specific data, sources or economic indicators to support the claim that Germany was close to bankruptcy or “disappearance“. It is in line with his previous attacks on Germany's energy transition and his argument that renewables are unreliable and make electricity more expensive.
What the data shows for Germany
Official German statistics show that renewables provided 58.6% of the electricity produced and fed into the grid in 2025. The share of renewable energy in gross electricity consumption was 55.1%, the German Environment Agency reported.
Wind power remained the country's leading source of electricity, and photovoltaic production reached a new annual record. Germany also continues to use coal, natural gas and other conventional sources, but their share in the electricity mix is smaller than that of renewables.
The country is indeed going through a prolonged period of economic weakness. Gross domestic product shrank in 2023 and 2024, but grew by 0.2% in 2025, according to data from the German statistics office “Destatis“. This means stagnation and a slow recovery, not state bankruptcy.
The energy transition debate
Trump has used Germany as an example in his criticism of policies to reduce carbon emissions. In September 2025, he told the UN General Assembly that the country had “gone green and gone bankrupt“. At the time, German and international media pointed out that his assessment mixed Germany's real economic problems with a political dispute over the energy transition and did not correspond to official macroeconomic data.
Berlin has set a goal of renewables providing at least 80% of gross electricity consumption by 2030. The Trump administration is following the opposite course in Washington, promoting coal, oil and natural gas production, as well as the development of nuclear energy. The White House declared October 2026 as “Energy Dominance Month“ and presented reliable baseload capacity as a priority for the American economy.

articles.title: France is devouring itself as school riots reveal a crisis far bigger than broken classrooms - Fox News
articles.summary: France is devouring itself as school riots reveal a crisis far bigger than broken classrooms  Fox News
articles.full_text:
Student protests over crumbling schools despite billions in public spending are fueling a broader crisis in France, and experts warn that the country's mounting financial troubles, President Emmanuel Macron's weakened political center and radical movements are pushing the unrest far beyond its original educational grievances.
Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, the Foundation for Defense of Democracies' senior envoy for Europe, told Fox News Digital in an interview from Paris that what began in September with legitimate complaints about school conditions has increasingly been exploited by political forces seeking confrontation with the state.
"Overall, I'd say the anger is real, but the violence, I would say, is organized," she said, adding that destroying schools would do nothing to improve the education system.
Seventy-two percent of education expenditures went toward salaries, social contributions and pensions for teaching and non-teaching personnel, while just 8.5% went toward investment, including infrastructure and equipment. The figures cover the entire education system, not just high schools, according to France's Education Ministry's 2026 statistical overview.
Harvey Feigenbaum, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University and an expert on French politics, told Fox News Digital that France's underlying problem is a government caught between expensive social commitments, sluggish economic growth and mounting pressure to cut spending.
"France is in deep debt. It wants to cut its expenses," Feigenbaum said, explaining that years of financial pressure and neglected school facilities have fueled frustration among students.
The scale of the financial predicament is striking. According to Eurostat, French public debt stood at 117.6% of GDP in the first quarter of 2026, the third-highest ratio in the European Union, behind Greece and Italy.
Reuters reported Oct. 8 that rising borrowing costs and investor concerns have severely limited the government's ability to resolve unrest through additional spending, a strategy employed during previous waves of French protests.
The financial squeeze has collided with an increasingly fragmented political system, creating opportunities for parties at both ends of the political spectrum to capitalize on public dissatisfaction.
Macron's political center collapses
For Feigenbaum, the long-term roots of the crisis lie in Macron's political legacy.
When Macron won the presidency in 2017, he promised to move beyond France's traditional left-right divide, combining policies from both sides into a new centrist political movement.
But Feigenbaum argues that the strategy produced an unintended consequence, weakening France's established moderate parties without creating a durable governing coalition to replace them.
"What he ended up doing was attracting the moderate voters from the parties of the moderate left and the parties from the moderate right, and essentially destroyed those parties," Feigenbaum said.
He argued that the collapse of the traditional political center helped create space for more ideologically polarized movements.
"Macron is a smart man, but he's a terrible politician," the professor added.
Macron's controversial pension reforms illustrate the difficulty of persuading French voters to accept reductions in longstanding public benefits, Feigenbaum argued. Those efforts triggered widespread protests, while implementation of the 2023 retirement changes has since been suspended until 2028.
The situation became especially difficult after Macron called snap parliamentary elections in 2024, producing a deeply divided National Assembly without a governing majority.
"Even if the government wanted to do something coherent, they simply don't have the votes to do it," Feigenbaum said.
That paralysis has left Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu handling the immediate unrest while Macron faces questions about the stability of the political system he helped reshape.
Why are France's schools struggling despite billions in spending?
The protests began in the Paris suburbs in September amid complaints about overcrowded classrooms, inadequate heating and cooling, aging buildings and teachers who were not replaced when absent.
Rodan-Benzaquen said the anger reflected years of educational instability, frequent ministerial changes and reforms that have failed to resolve persistent school problems.
She also pointed to a broader sense of anxiety among young people about their economic future, artificial intelligence, climate change and international conflicts.
According to the OECD's September 2026 Education at a Glance report, France spent $16,674 in funding per student in general upper secondary education in 2023, compared with an OECD average of $12,421, adjusted for purchasing power.
Yet teachers and students continue to complain about basic shortages.
Responsibility for public high school buildings and equipment falls to regional authorities, while the national government oversees much of the education system, including teacher staffing.
Feigenbaum said France's centralized education structure makes national leaders the focus of public anger when schools fail to deliver.
The pressure has already forced a concession.
Reuters reported Friday that Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced an emergency plan to deploy 3,000 qualified educators to particularly affected schools, costing several dozen million euros.
Student unions welcomed the measure as an initial victory but pledged to continue demonstrating.
The spending figures raise broader questions about whether France's financial and political priorities have left sufficient resources for maintaining school infrastructure and meeting students' needs. They do not, however, establish that teachers' unions or other organized constituencies have improperly diverted funding.
How the far left entered the unrest
As the demonstrations expanded, the involvement of France's hard-left La France Insoumise party, known as LFI, led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, became an increasingly contentious issue.
Reuters reported Oct. 1 that French intelligence agencies had told a government crisis meeting that LFI and affiliated activists played a role in fomenting the unrest. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez also cited agitators moving between schools to encourage violence.
LFI has denied responsibility and accused authorities of aggravating tensions through their response.
Rodan-Benzaquen said far-left movements were capitalizing on students' frustration.
"There is an obvious instrumentalization, obvious manipulation," she said, arguing that activists were seeking to push some protesters toward violence.
She linked the unrest to what she described as Mélenchon's broader political strategy ahead of France's 2027 presidential election.
"His idea is that, on the one hand, he will scare voters on the right and on the far right, who will then go to vote for the far right, and, on the other hand, he would mobilize his own camp," she said.
Rodan-Benzaquen argued that intensifying political confrontation could help Mélenchon consolidate his support among younger voters and immigrant communities, while portraying the far right as an increasingly serious threat.
She described it as a calculated political strategy rather than a spontaneous response to students' concerns.
The involvement of LFI politicians has been documented by French media, although there is disagreement over whether the party helped initiate the demonstrations or became involved after the protests began.
An Oct. 2 investigation by Le Monde examined a police intelligence assessment describing radical left activity around schools in Seine-Saint-Denis but questioned whether the evidence established that the movement itself was politically orchestrated.
Feigenbaum offered a more cautious interpretation, describing some of the violent perpetrators as fringe provocateurs who exploit broader demonstrations without necessarily directing them.
"They're not being organized by some, you know, some mastermind at the national level, at least as far as anyone knows," he said.
Islamist influence or political solidarity?
The demonstrations have also raised questions about whether Islamist groups and pro-Palestinian activists are seeking to use the unrest to advance broader ideological causes.
Rodan-Benzaquen argued that Mélenchon's emphasis on Gaza and the Palestinian cause has helped bring together political constituencies that might otherwise have little in common.
"It's sort of the idea of sort of an intersection of different movements where they manage to bring together the different groups, the far left, Islamist movements, pro-Palestinian activists," she said.
She pointed to Palestinian flags appearing during the demonstrations as an indication of how the movement has expanded beyond its original educational demands.
The FDD expert argued that Islamist elements were attempting to capitalize on the turmoil, although she cautioned against reducing the entire crisis to immigration or religion.
"But this goes far beyond the issue of immigration. It goes far beyond the issue of Islamism. It goes far beyond the issue of Islam," she said.
A crisis France cannot simply spend its way out of

Investing.com -- Growing fiscal risks in France could prompt the European Central Bank to pause interest rate hikes after December, or earlier if financial stress spreads across the eurozone, according to Citi analysts.
Citi said the ECB is shifting its focus towards financial conditions from inflation concerns, raising questions about how much further it can tighten monetary policy.
The bank's rates strategists highlighted a reversal in the relationship between ECB rate expectations and the spread between French and German government bond yields, suggesting markets increasingly view policy as overly restrictive.
A December rate increase is almost fully priced in, alongside nearly two further hikes in 2027, according to Citi.
The bank sees scope for 50 to 75 basis points of repricing in ECB rates relative to the U.S. Federal Reserve as investors reassess the outlook.
That shift could weaken the euro, particularly if concerns about French public finances increase the risk premium on eurozone assets.
Citi's foreign exchange strategists said EUR/USD could fall below 1.10 if the currency undershoots fair value implied by two-year interest rate differentials.
Its two-year valuation model suggests a 50 to 75 basis point reduction in the euro-U.S. rate spread could push EUR/USD towards 1.1075 to 1.1000, even without an additional undershoot.
Citi identified receiving ECB rates against Fed rates as its preferred trade, arguing the position could remain attractive if tensions involving Iran ease.
Lower commodity prices following an Iran resolution could support French equities, government bonds and the euro, making outright bearish positions in those assets less attractive.
Citi's analysis suggests that fiscal uncertainty and a more accommodative ECB response could both pressure the euro, leaving the currency vulnerable to further declines as investors reassess the central bank's policy outlook.

articles.title: With new frigates and naval bases: Germany arms its navy for war against Russia - World Socialist Web Site
articles.summary: With new frigates and naval bases: Germany arms its navy for war against Russia  World Socialist Web Site
articles.full_text:
The German government is rapidly advancing the rearmament of the German Navy and preparations for a direct war against Russia. Within a matter of days, plans for a new naval base in Emden, the procurement of eight frigates costing approximately €11.6 billion, and the multibillion-euro expansion of Bremerhaven into a NATO military logistics hub were announced or further specified. These decisions are part of Germany’s comprehensive transition to a war footing and underscore Berlin’s ambition to assume an increasingly leading military role within NATO.
The measures come amid NATO’s continuing escalation of its confrontation with Russia despite explicit nuclear warnings from Moscow. While Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) announced the development and delivery of additional long-range weapons systems in Kiev in early October, the Bundeswehr is creating the military infrastructure for a large-scale war that could extend from the Baltic Sea across the North Atlantic and deep into Russian territory.
On October 5, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius (SPD) announced at a press conference in Emden the decision to establish a second major North Sea base for the German Navy, alongside Wilhelmshaven, at Rysumer Nacken on the Ems estuary. The planned facility will cover up to 450 hectares, have approximately five kilometres of piers and accommodate up to 2,000 military and civilian personnel. Among other things, berths are planned for seven frigates, ten minesweepers and ten tugboats.
The investment costs will run into billions of euros. The base is expected to achieve initial operational capability in the early 2030s, with full operational capability targeted for 2033 or 2034. So far, a declaration of intent has been signed; the precise design of the facilities and the final deployment of ships have yet to be determined.
Pistorius left no doubt about the military objectives. Germany currently has the smallest navy in the history of the Bundeswehr, while facing the broadest range of missions. The navy therefore has to grow, and it will grow. Along with the Baltic Sea, the North Sea and North Atlantic were of decisive strategic importance.
The new Chief of the Navy, Vice Admiral Wilhelm Tobias Abry, explicitly identified the North Sea and North Atlantic as priority areas for the German Navy within NATO defence planning. The second base is intended to create additional capacity for operations, logistics and the deployment of military forces. Warships currently stationed in the Baltic Sea must also be capable of being transferred to the North Sea if necessary in the event of war.
Pistorius also stressed that distributing the fleet across several locations would increase its operational capabilities in a crisis. This is therefore not merely about additional berths, but about creating a decentralised military infrastructure capable of remaining operational under wartime conditions. Emden’s civilian port facilities could also explicitly be used for troop deployments.
Just three days later, on October 8, the Bundestag’s Budget Committee approved the procurement of four additional MEKO A-200 DEU frigates, after four ships had already been authorised in July. This brings the planned total to eight of these warships, which specialise in anti-submarine warfare, to be procured from TKMS.
According to current figures, the first four frigates will cost approximately €6.3 billion, with the additional four costing another €5.3 billion. The first ship is scheduled for delivery at the end of 2029, with the remaining vessels to follow in quick succession. They will replace the originally planned F126-class frigates, whose procurement was discontinued following problems with the Dutch Damen shipyard.
According to the Defence Ministry, the frigates are intended primarily for deployment in the North Sea and Baltic Sea regions, the Atlantic and the High North. Their central task is to combat enemy submarines—particularly as part of NATO operations against Russia’s Northern Fleet and to secure control over the strategic sea lanes between North America and Europe.
“Fight tonight. Fight tomorrow.”
The war plans underlying these decisions are revealed in the strategic document Kurs Marine (“Navy Course”), published by the Bundeswehr in May 2025. The approximately 40-page document is a detailed blueprint for transforming Germany’s naval forces for a major war, particularly against Russia.
The military-geographical analysis alone is revealing. The document identifies the North Atlantic, including the Norwegian Sea, as well as the North Sea and Baltic Sea as central areas of operation. Particular importance is attached to the so-called GIUK Gap between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is strategically significant for monitoring Russian submarines and securing NATO’s transatlantic supply routes.
The strategic planning extends from the American Atlantic coast to the eastern Baltic Sea. In a war against Russia, enormous numbers of American and European troops, weapons and quantities of ammunition would have to be transported to Europe by sea and then moved to the front.
However, the navy is by no means planning only defensive escort and protection operations. The strategy paper explicitly calls for disrupting and cutting off enemy supply routes as far as their ports. Under the heading Maritime Strike, it also describes the capability to launch long-range attacks from warships and submarines against military targets deep inland.
In the Baltic Sea, the navy is to use these capabilities to attack enemy missile positions and other military installations on land. Alongside larger warships, unmanned systems, drones and smaller platforms—that are difficult to detect—are envisaged for these operations.
The naval infantry is also being reorganised for offensive operations. Instead of concentrating on protection and security duties, it is to be capable of seizing and controlling militarily significant coastal areas, islands and ports. The document explicitly calls for a reorientation toward offensive operations in the Baltic Sea region.
The entire fleet is being geared toward these tasks. The original force structure envisaged for 2035 includes six F127 air-defence frigates, six F126 anti-submarine frigates, three to four F125 frigates, nine to twelve submarines, numerous corvettes, minehunters and combat boats, as well as large numbers of unmanned surface, underwater and aerial systems. The new MEKO procurement alters these original plans but maintains the fundamental orientation toward large-scale naval warfare.
The timetable is decisive. Under the heading “Fight tonight. Fight tomorrow,” the naval leadership demands both the long-term construction of a powerful fleet and the immediate achievement of the highest possible level of war readiness. The existing forces are to become significantly more capable by 2029.
To achieve this, ships are to be deployed more frequently and for longer periods, their armaments strengthened, ammunition stocks increased, and new systems introduced through accelerated procurement or leasing. In future, two-thirds of the fleet are to be maintained at high or full operational readiness at all times—instead of the current situation in which only one-third is fully combat-ready.
Naval infrastructure is also to be prepared for every phase of escalation in a conflict. New bases, decentralised command structures, protected shipyards, depots and arsenals are intended to ensure that the navy can continue fighting even under direct attack.
The document concludes with a remarkably explicit instruction to all personnel: “peacetime operations” are a thing of the past. In other words, the navy is now operating in “wartime mode.” It must be able to prove itself in battle. The final sentence reads: “It is not ships that fight, but people.”
German ports as military logistics hubs
The new base in Emden is a direct implementation of these strategic objectives. The same applies to the expansion of Bremerhaven into the so-called Deployment Hub Bremerhaven 2031.
On September 29, Pistorius, Bremen Mayor Andreas Bovenschulte (SPD) and representatives of the port logistics company BLG signed a declaration of intent for the project. By 2031, approximately €1.35 billion is earmarked in the federal defence budget for port, transport and airport infrastructure suitable for military use. This is supplemented by more than €212 million from Bremen’s special port infrastructure fund.
The plans include new heavy-load handling areas and bridges, upgrades to quays and harbour basins, and the expansion of transport connections. Bremen Airport is also part of the programme.
The objective is to transport large numbers of American and other NATO troops, together with tanks, ammunition and heavy military equipment, through Germany to the alliance’s eastern flank. Pistorius explicitly stated that, in a crisis, tens of thousands of soldiers would have to be supplied in Bremerhaven on their way east.
These measures implement central provisions of the secret and continuously updated Operations Plan Germany (Operationsplan Deutschland). It specifies how government agencies, businesses, transport infrastructure and civilian organisations are to support the Bundeswehr and allied armed forces in periods of heightened tension and war.
The extent to which preparations have already advanced was demonstrated in late September by the Red Storm Charlie exercise in Hamburg. From September 24 to 26, approximately 1,700 members of the Bundeswehr, government agencies, civilian relief organisations and businesses jointly rehearsed military troop movements and responses to sabotage, drone attacks and other threats to infrastructure. Even Hamburg’s harbour ferries were incorporated into the simulated troop movements.

President Donald Trump told a crowd of his most loyal MAGA supporters in Tennessee that he could “say the stupidest things” and they’d still clap — as Republicans ramp up their campaigning ahead of the midterm elections.
The 80-year-old president appeared at a rally in Clarksville, about 50 miles northwest of Nashville, to “supercharge” his loyal supporters on Saturday, according to the Republican National Committee.
Trump’s MAGA base didn’t seem fazed by his blunt remarks, or even as he questioned why he was even campaigning in the state since Sen. Bill Hagerty and Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who is running for governor, are both polling ahead in their respective races.
“What am I doing in Tennessee?” Trump asked the crowd. “I don’t have to campaign here. I’ve won your state by many, many, many points. Some ridiculous number. All the time.”
He continued: “So, three times I won the election, the big election three times. I got screwed the second time because they cheated. They cheated. We cannot let that happen again.”
“But, I said, ‘You know, sometimes it’s nice to go to a place where you don’t have to be, but you are there to say thank you to the great people that elected you three separate times,” he said to roaring applause.
Trump then told the story of a “friend” who has stage fright and asked him how he does rallies in front of thousands of people.
“I said, ‘You know, for me it’s easy because there is such love in these rooms,” Trump said to cheers and applause, before adding, “It’s true.”
The crowd then broke out into chanting, “Trump, Trump, Trump!”
“No, it’s true. No, there’s such love,” he said, as MAGA devotees cried out, “We love you!”
“It’s like, like, I mean, it’s amazing. When you stand up here, it’s like, the love,” Trump continued. “I could say the stupidest things, and you’d clap. ‘Oh, I love you so — it’s true.”
“But we don’t say the stupidest things; we say things of common sense,” Trump claimed. “We say things that make sense, and probably are mostly conservative. But it’s not really conservative; it’s the things of common sense.
“We want to have a border, we want to have low taxes, we want to have a great military. We want to have, you know, all of the different things. It’s like seven, eight, 10, five, four — it’s just things that are common sense,” he rambled.
At the end of his speech, held Saturday afternoon at F&M Bank Arena, Trump welcomed the Republicans on the ballot to the stage and urged attendees to go to the polls and vote for them.
“I’m on the ballot — just pretend I’m on the ballot,” he said, repeating a desperate plea he has made numerous times while campaigning, including in several key states just last week.
While Trump may not be on the ballot this Election Day, some Americans are shying away from him and the candidates he has backed over issues like the war in Iran, high gas prices and inflation.
A recent Politico poll found that 26 percent of 2024 Trump voters believe GOP candidates in their district have a better shot at winning their midterm elections if they broke with the president. Meanwhile, 62 percent of MAGA believe GOP candidates in their district have a better chance of winning if they align with Trump.
